desc:
There are k lists of closed intervals with integer endpoints, numbered 0 to k - 1. All their intervals are stored together in intervals as triples [list, start, end], in arbitrary order. Inside one list the intervals are disjoint and do not even touch: if two of them belong to the same list, one ends strictly before the other starts. A list may have no triples at all.

Return the set of points (real numbers) that lie in every one of the k lists, as a sorted list of closed intervals [a, b] with a ≤ b. A single shared point gives [a, a].

k = 2
list 0: [0,2] [5,10] [13,23] [24,25]
list 1: [1,5] [8,12] [15,24] [25,26]
intervals = [[0,0,2], [0,5,10], [0,13,23], [0,24,25],
             [1,1,5], [1,8,12], [1,15,24], [1,25,26]]
result    = [[1,2], [5,5], [8,10], [15,23], [24,24], [25,25]]
constraints: Within one list, the next start is greater than the previous end
hints: Intersecting two lists with two pointers is the standard approach. Is there a way to handle all k lists at once?
Count, for a moving point, how many intervals cover it. Because the intervals of one list never overlap, the count equals the number of lists covering that point.

Sweep over all start and end events sorted by position (starts before ends at the same position, since the intervals are closed). A common piece begins when the count reaches k and ends at the next end event while the count is k.
editorial: Turn every interval into two events: a start at start and an end at end. Sort the events by position and, at equal positions, put starts before ends, because closed intervals that share an endpoint still share that point. Walk through the events with a counter of currently open intervals. Since the intervals of a single list are pairwise disjoint, no list can contribute more than one open interval at a time, so the counter is the number of lists that cover the current point.

When a start event raises the counter to k, remember its position as the left end of a common piece. When an end event arrives while the counter equals k, the piece closes at that position; then decrement the counter. Pieces that merely touch cannot occur, because that would need some list to have two touching intervals. With m intervals in total the sort costs O(m log m); the sweep is linear. Folding the lists pairwise with the two-pointer intersection works as well but needs sorted lists first.
